title: World Elevation Atlas: Sample Any Point on Earth
description: Sample a 7×7 grid of real elevations around any point with the World Elevation Atlas — from Everest's 8,849 m to the Dead Sea's shore. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the atlas's ceiling is Everest at 8,849 metres (29,032 ft) and its floor is the Dead Sea shore at roughly −430 metres (−1,411 ft) — every sampled point on Earth lives between those two published extremes.
quick_answer: The World Elevation Atlas samples a 7×7 grid of real elevations around any point on Earth, so you can read a place's height pattern rather than a single number. Set a centre, choose an area size, and read forty-nine elevations at once — the neighbourhood's relief in one view.
steps_intro: One point's elevation is a fact; forty-nine are a landscape:

body.t: Planning in unfamiliar country — a trek, a site, a purchase — starts with how the land rises. The
turns the same kind of sampling into slopes.
Two candidate towns, two grids: the spread between a grid's lowest and highest cells is the place's relief personality in one glance.
A suspicious elevation from one source gets cross-examined by its neighbours. Terrain is continuous; a cell that disagrees with all forty-eight neighbours is the dataset clearing its throat.
Sample the Nile delta, the Tibetan Plateau's edge and the Netherlands in one lesson — relief stops being a colour scale and becomes numbers students can argue with.

Denver's official elevation is 5,280 feet by civic pride and about 1,609 metres by survey — 'mile high' within a rounding of the published figure. An atlas grid around the city shows the plains' gentle rise toward the foothills instead.

Sample the Dead Sea shore and the grid returns negative elevations around −430 m — land below the ocean's level, protected by geography. Death Valley's Badwater Basin reads about −86 m on the same scale.

popular_table.note: Grid values come from global terrain-model sampling (via the elevation API), which smooths sharp peaks and narrow ridges — a sampled Everest cell can read lower than the surveyed summit. Published point surveys outrank grid samples at famous points.

faq: How accurate are the grid elevations?

They inherit the source terrain model's accuracy — typically a few metres in gentle country, coarser on cliffs and narrow ridges. Fine for relief reading; not a substitute for a survey where a boundary or a building depends on it.
Why a 7×7 grid instead of one point?
Terrain questions are pattern questions. Forty-nine samples expose slope direction, drainage hints and dataset oddities that one number hides — at the cost of nothing but a wider click.
Ocean cells in elevation models generally read at or near sea level (bathymetry is usually outside these land models), so read sea cells as 'surface', not as seabed depth.
Match the question: a property wants hundreds of metres across; a mountain range wants tens of kilometres. The same grid logic serves both — cell spacing scales with the area you pick.
Why can the atlas disagree with my GPS altitude?

GPS altitude is ellipsoidal and noisy (often ±10–30 m vertically in consumer gear); the atlas is a terrain model tied to sea level. A disagreement of a few metres is normal; a hundred metres is a story worth investigating.
The land surface spans Everest's 8,849 m down to the Dead Sea shore near −430 m — both published survey figures. Any grid value outside that span is a data error, not a discovery.
Can I sample the poles or mid-ocean islands?
Yes — the atlas is global. Polar and island grids work wherever the underlying model has coverage, which for modern global terrain data is effectively everywhere on land.
